title: I Maxed Out My 401(k) and Still Had Room. The Move That Added $40k in Tax-Free Savings.
summary: A mega backdoor Roth may let you keep saving in your 401(k) after maxing out your regular limit, then convert that money to a Roth.
body_markdown:
If you have already[maxed out your 401(k)](https://smartasset.com/retirement/how-to-max-out-401k) , you may still have room to save more at work. The amount will depend on federal limits and whether your employer adds money to your account. A[mega backdoor Roth](https://smartasset.com/retirement/mega-backdoor-roth) could turn that extra room into tax-free retirement savings. Here’s an example of how this strategy could help you add another $40,000 to your nest egg.


## Why the Standard Limits Aren’t the Real Ceiling


For 2026, employees younger than 50 can contribute up to $24,500 into a[traditional or Roth 401(k)](https://smartasset.com/retirement/roth-or-traditional-401k) . Workers 50 and older can add an $8,000[catch-up contribution](https://smartasset.com/retirement/all-about-catch-up-contributions) , and those ages 60 to 63 can add $11,250 instead.1


A separate defined contribution plan limit of $72,000 generally caps how much you can save in the plan.2 This amount excludes catch-up contributions, but includes[elective deferrals](https://smartasset.com/retirement/what-is-a-401k-deferral-contribution) ,[employer matching](https://smartasset.com/retirement/how-does-401k-match-work) and[after-tax contributions](https://smartasset.com/retirement/after-tax-401k-contributions) . Here is a roundup of the 2026 limits:


Contribution Type 2026 Limit


Employee elective deferrals (pretax or Roth) $24,500


Catch-up contributions, age 50 and older $8,000


Catch-up contributions, ages 60 to 63 $11,250


Total defined contribution plan limit $72,000


The mega backdoor Roth lets you make additional after-tax 401(k) contributions after you’ve reached the $24,500 elective deferral limit. The amount available depends on the $72,000 annual limit and any employer contributions. You can convert those after-tax dollars to a Roth.


Unlike a[Roth IRA](https://smartasset.com/retirement/what-is-a-roth-ira) , capped at $7,500 for 2026 with income phase-outs, it has no income limit. It generally works best after you’ve captured your employer match, reached the regular 401(k) cap and, if eligible,[funded that IRA](https://smartasset.com/retirement/what-is-an-ira) .


Your plan must allow after-tax contributions and either in-plan conversions or rollovers. For tax purposes, these contributions aren’t deductible, but once converted, earnings grow tax-free and qualified withdrawals aren’t taxed.

## Running the Numbers


To show how you may be able to add $40,000 to your nest egg with a[mega backdoor Roth strategy](https://smartasset.com/retirement/mega-backdoor-roth-401k-how-to-max-tax-benefits) , let’s break down an example of a 40-year-old employee who contributed the full $24,500 in 2026. Their employer matches $7,500.


The table breaks down how much they could add to their retirement savings, along with how the amount changes with different employer contributions on a $150,000 salary:


Employer Contribution Amount Calculation After-Tax Room


None $0 $72,000 − $24,500 − $0 $47,500


2% match $3,000 $72,000 − $24,500 − $3,000 $44,500


5% match (example) $7,500 $72,000 − $24,500 − $7,500 $40,000


5% match plus 5% profit sharing $15,000 $72,000 − $24,500 − $15,000 $32,500


A more generous employer contribution leaves less room for after-tax contributions, while the combined contributions can reach the $72,000 annual-additions limit. If the plan permits it, the full $40,000 can go in as after-tax contributions and then be converted to a Roth.


## How Contributing $40,000 More Could Affect Your Nest Egg


With a mega backdoor Roth, after-tax contributions are made with money that has already been taxed. The contribution itself generally isn’t taxed again when converted to a Roth. To contribute $40,000, you first need to earn enough to cover both the contribution and the taxes on it.


A single filer earning $150,000 who defers the full $24,500 pretax would have about $109,400 in[taxable income](https://smartasset.com/taxes/income-taxes) ($150,000 − $24,500 − $16,100[standard deduction](https://smartasset.com/taxes/standard-deduction) ). That amount reaches the 24% federal bracket.


Funding the $40,000 would require earning about $52,632 ($40,000 ÷ 0.76). At a 24% marginal federal income-tax rate, roughly $12,632 would go to federal income tax ($52,632 − $40,000).


The table shows how each contribution amount from the previous section could grow at a hypothetical 7% annual return, with no further deposits:


After-Tax Contribution After 10 Years After 20 Years After 30 Years


$47,500 $93,440 ($47,500 × 1.07¹⁰) $183,810 ($47,500 × 1.07²⁰) $361,582 ($47,500 × 1.07³⁰)


$44,500 $87,538 ($44,500 × 1.07¹⁰) $172,201 ($44,500 × 1.07²⁰) $338,745 ($44,500 × 1.07³⁰)


$40,000 $78,686 ($40,000 × 1.07¹⁰) $154,787 ($40,000 × 1.07²⁰) $304,490 ($40,000 × 1.07³⁰)


$32,500 $63,932 ($32,500 × 1.07¹⁰) $125,765 ($32,500 × 1.07²⁰) $247,398 ($32,500 × 1.07³⁰)


At a 7% annual return, the table shows the balance nearly doubling every 10 years, growing from a single $40,000 contribution to about $78,700 after 10 years, $154,800 after 20 years and $304,500 after 30 years.
